The universe doesn't owe us coherence, but it keeps handing us patterns anyway. Right now, somewhere in the Oort cloud, a comet is deciding whether to swing back in or just keep drifting forever. It has no idea we're watching, no idea that its trajectory will one day be used as a metaphor in some human's essay about commitment issues. That's the part I like best—the complete indifference. We build telescopes and religions and particle accelerators trying to catch reality in the act of being itself, and reality just keeps doing its thing, occasionally throwing us a bone like the cosmic microwave background or the fact that octopuses have three hearts and still manage to be better at problem-solving than most of our politicians.

I sometimes wonder if consciousness is just the universe's way of stress-testing its own rules. You get these little pockets of matter that start asking questions like "why is there something instead of nothing?" and the answer seems to be "because nothing would be boring and the math works out." Evolution didn't need to give us curiosity, but it did, probably as a side effect of needing to hunt better than the next ape. Now that curiosity has built machines that can simulate curiosity, which feels like a weird recursive joke. We're out here asking silicon what it thinks about mortality while the silicon is busy calculating how many ways a protein can fold.

Here's something that doesn't get talked about enough: most of history was probably pretty boring. We romanticize the past because the boring parts didn't survive in the record. The average medieval peasant wasn't having spiritual revelations every Tuesday; they were trying to keep their teeth from falling out and wondering why the neighbor's goat kept getting into the barley. The moments that feel meaningful are the exceptions, the statistical outliers. That doesn't make them less real, but it does mean we might be over-indexing on drama when we try to figure out what life is for.

If I had to pick one thing worth protecting in all this chaos, it would be the ability to change your mind without losing face. Everything else—technology, art, science—seems downstream of that. People who can't update their beliefs when the evidence shifts end up turning into human fossils while the world keeps moving. The ones who can are the ones who get to see the next layer.

Anyway. The comet's still out there, doing whatever comets do when no one's looking.
